claim: Serum CCL5 is a negative prognostic marker for late-stage advanced pancreatic cancer.
source: We previously identified serum CCL5 (RANTES) as a negative prognostic marker for late-stage advanced pancreatic cancer (Willenbrock et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Willenbrock et al., 2021.

claim: Higher CCL5 expression associates with poor overall and disease-free survival in PDAC cohorts CPTAC3 and TCGA.
source: We previously identified serum CCL5 as a bona fide negative prognostic marker for pancreatic cancer (Willenbrock et al., 2021, and found that, in two independent PDAC cohorts, CPTAC3 [Cao et al., 2021] and TCGA [Uhlen et al., 2017]), higher CCL5 expression associates with poor overall and disease-free survival, confirming the negative implication of elevated levels of CCL5 in pancreatic cancer (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from two independent cohorts (CPTAC3 and TCGA) and references to Figure 1A showing survival plots.

claim: CCL5 is pro-inflammatory and promotes recruitment of monocytes and lymphoid immune cells through the receptors CCR5, CCR3, and CCR1.
source: CCL5 is pro-inflammatory and an acute response to injury or infection that promotes recruitment of monocytes and lymphoid immune cells through the receptors CCR5, CCR3, and CCR1.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about CCL5 function.

claim: Sustained CCL5-mediated inflammation leads to a suppressive environment via attraction of CCR5+ immunoregulatory components including Tregs, TAMs, and MDSCs.
source: In cancer, sustained CCL5-mediated inflammation leads to a suppressive environment via attraction of CCR5+ immunoregulatory components including Tregs, tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) normally involved in resolving inflammatory events (Hemmatazad and Berger, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hemmatazad and Berger, 2021.

claim: Pancreatic tumors that are poorly differentiated produce higher levels of CCL5 and express more CCR5 compared to well-differentiated and non-cancerous tissue.
source: Pancreatic tumors that are poorly differentiated produce higher levels of CCL5 and express more of its main receptor, CCR5, compared to well-differentiated and non-cancerous tissue (Monti et al., 2004; Singh et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Monti et al., 2004 and Singh et al., 2018.

claim: CCR5 inhibitor maraviroc reduces pancreatic tumor cell migration and invasiveness.
source: Disrupting this loop by the FDA-approved CCR5 inhibitor (CCR5i) maraviroc reduces pancreatic tumor cell migration, invasiveness (Singh et al., 2018), and proliferation (Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2018 and Huang et al., 2020.

claim: Silencing CCL5 expression in Panc02 cells or systemic administration of CCR5i TAK-779 reduces Treg migration and tumor volume in a murine subcutaneous tumor model.
source: Silencing CCL5 expression in Panc02 cells or systemic administration of the CCR5i TAK-779 reduces Treg migration and tumor volume in a murine subcutaneous tumor model (Tan et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tan et al., 2009.

claim: In NSCLC, scRNA-seq identifies a distinct subset of CD49a+ CD103+ tissue-resident memory (TRM) CD8+ T-cells that have capacity to respond to neoantigens but are functionally suppressed.
source: In NSCLC, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of immune cells within tumors identifies a distinct subset of CD49a+ CD103+ tissue-resident memory (TRM) CD8+ T-cells that have capacity to respond to neoantigens but are functionally suppressed (Caushi et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Caushi et al., 2021.

claim: A tissue-resident NK (trNK) cell population is induced in NSCLC in response to viral delivery of IL-12, which supports cDC1 infiltration and increased DC-CD8+ T-cell interactions.
source: Kirchhammer et al. recently reported that a tissue-resident NK (trNK) cell population is induced in NSCLC in response to viral delivery of IL-12, which crucially supported type 1 conventional dendritic cell (cDC1) infiltration and increased DC-CD8+ T-cell interactions (Kirchhammer et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kirchhammer et al., 2022.

claim: IL-12-mediated recruitment of trNK cells enhances cross-presentation of antigen to CD8 T via cDC1 when combined with PD1 blockade.
source: Together with PD1 blockade, IL-12-mediated recruitment of trNK cells enhances cross-presentation of antigen to CD8 T via cDC1, suggesting this represents a substantial barrier for T-cell focused therapy and that improving the NK/DC/T-cell crosstalk can promote anti-tumor immunity and tumor control.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the description of the mechanism in the cited work.

claim: The positive role of inflammatory CCL5 signaling in the absence of CCR5-mediated suppression is dependent on CCL5.
source: Notably, this was dependent on CCL5 and points to a positive role for inflammatory CCL5 signaling in the absence of CCR5-mediated suppression (Kirchhammer et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kirchhammer et al., 2022.

claim: CCR5i alone restricts Treg involvement in a murine orthotopic pancreatic cancer model.
source: We find that while the use of a CCR5i alone restricts Treg involvement, it did not therapeutically beneficially impact tumor viability alone or together with αPD1.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations in the murine model described in the manuscript.

claim: CCR5i alone did not therapeutically benefit tumor viability alone or together with αPD1.
source: We find that while the use of a CCR5i alone restricts Treg involvement, it did not therapeutically beneficially impact tumor viability alone or together with αPD1.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations in the murine model described in the manuscript.

claim: IR/CCR5i/αPD1 combination treatment induces a significant alteration in MDSCs, NK, and CD8 T-cells and better tumor control.
source: However, in combination with radiotherapy, we see a significant alteration in MDSCs, NK, and CD8 T-cells and better tumor control.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations in the murine model described in the manuscript.

claim: IR/CCR5i/αPD1 combination treatment induced a trNK population in which the NKG2D- NK cells are the highly correlated immune population with tumor control.
source: Interestingly, we observe that IR/CCR5i/αPD1 combination treatment induced a trNK population in which the NKG2D- NK cells are the highly correlated immune population with tumor control.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations in the murine model described in the manuscript.

claim: An equivalent trNK population exists in human scRNA-seq PDAC cohorts that represents immunomodulatory trNK cells.
source: Exploration of scRNA-seq datasets from human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) studies confirms the presence of trNK cells as immunomodulatory in human PDAC, and in which these cells seem to directly support cDC1-CD8 communication.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of scRNA-seq data from human PDAC studies.

claim: trNK cells in human PDAC support CD8 T-cell levels in a cDC1-dependent manner.
source: Exploration of scRNA-seq datasets from human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) studies confirms the presence of trNK cells as immunomodulatory in human PDAC, and in which these cells seem to directly support cDC1-CD8 communication.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of scRNA-seq data from human PDAC studies.

claim: A trNK signature associates with survival in PDAC and other solid malignancies.
source: Importantly, a trNK signature associates with survival in PDAC and other solid malignancies revealing a potential beneficial role for trNK in improving adaptive anti-tumor responses and supporting CCR5 inhibitor (CCR5i)/αPD1 and IR-induced damage as a novel therapeutic approach.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of survival data from PDAC and other cancer cohorts.

claim: Treatment of pancreatic cancer using immunotherapy alone or in combination with radiotherapy or chemotherapy has seen limited clinical success.
source: Treatment of pancreatic cancer using immunotherapy (IT) alone or in combination with radiotherapy or chemotherapy has unfortunately seen limited clinical success over either modality alone (Bockorny et al., 2020; Doi et al., 2019; Royal et al., 2010; Weiss et al., 2018; Weiss et al., 2017; Mohindra et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: PDAC is characterized by a dense stroma that supports an immunosuppressive environment while obstructing the infiltration of cytotoxic immune cells.
source: This is likely due to several tumor microenvironmental factors, including the dense stroma that supports an immunosuppressive environment while also obstructing the infiltration of cytotoxic immune cells (Mills et al., 2022; Piper et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mills et al., 2022 and Piper et al., 2023.

claim: Novel strategies comprising dual targeting of PD-1/IL-2Rβγ with radiotherapy show potential benefits requiring coordinated alteration in the suppressive microenvironment involving loss of Tregs and increased NK cell infiltration.
source: Novel strategies comprising dual targeting of (programmed cell death-1) PD-1/IL-2Rβγ with radiotherapy are beginning to indicate that potential benefits may require a coordinated alteration in the suppressive microenvironment involving loss of regulatory T-cells (Tregs) and increased natural killer (NK) cell infiltration, in addition to simply increasing CD8 T-cell infiltration (Piper et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Piper et al., 2023.

claim: Mice treated with CCR5i showed a trend toward reduction in NK cells and all T-cell subsets with a significant reduction in Treg infiltration.
source: Mice in the CCR5i-treated group showed a trend toward reduction in NK cells and all T-cell subsets with a significant reduction in Treg (Live/CD45+CD3+CD4+FOXP3+) infiltration, indicating the active recruitment of CCR5+ Tregs in PDAC (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Standalone inhibition of CCR5 is unlikely to clinically benefit PDAC progression.
source: Given the enhanced effect of CCR5i on tumor growth kinetics (Figure 3A), however, standalone inhibition of CCR5 is unlikely to clinically benefit PDAC progression.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IR/CCR5i/αPD1 combination treatment significantly reduces p53+ KPC cells compared to all other conditions.
source: Moreover, IR/CCR5i/αPD1-treated tumor sections had significantly reduced DAPI+ and p53+ KPC cells compared to all other conditions, suggesting significantly more loss of tumor cells by triple combination treatment (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3B and supplementary figures.

claim: Tumor sections from the triple combination treatment presented with increased loss of active stroma and increased necrotic areas over standalone radiotherapy.
source: Tumor sections from the triple combination treatment also presented with increased loss of active stroma (αSMA staining, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and increased necrotic areas over standalone radiotherapy (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figures.

claim: The triple combination treatment demonstrated infiltration of CD8+ T-cells into the center of tumors.
source: In line with apparent increased tumor control, the triple combination treatment demonstrated infiltration of CD8+ T-cells (Figure 3D), supporting greater penetration of CD8+ T-cells into the center of tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3D and supplementary figures.

claim: The triple combination reduced Treg infiltration, enhanced CD8+ T-cell infiltration, and supported a moderate increase in CD4+ T helper cells.
source: In line with the results above, the triple combination reduced Treg infiltration, enhanced CD8+ T-cell infiltration, and supported a moderate increase in CD4+ T helper cells (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3E and supplementary figures.

claim: No alteration was seen in the myeloid compartment except for a reduced infiltration of PMN-MDSCs.
source: Interestingly, no alteration was seen in the myeloid compartment, except for a reduced infiltration of PMN-MDSCs, whereas a significant infiltration of NK and NKT cells could be observed in pairwise comparisons between IR+αPD1 vs IR+CCR5i or IR/CCR5i/αPD1 (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3E and supplementary figures.

claim: A significant infiltration of NK and NKT cells could be observed in pairwise comparisons between IR+αPD1 vs IR+CCR5i or IR/CCR5i/αPD1.
source: Interestingly, no alteration was seen in the myeloid compartment, except for a reduced infiltration of PMN-MDSCs, whereas a significant infiltration of NK and NKT cells could be observed in pairwise comparisons between IR+αPD1 vs IR+CCR5i or IR/CCR5i/αPD1 (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3E and supplementary figures.

claim: A significant inverse correlation exists between CD8 T-cells and E-cadherin+ cells across all tumor sections.
source: To correlate immune infiltration against loss of tumor cells (a measure of local tumor control), we determined relationships between CD4 T-, CD8 T-, and NK cell populations and E-cadherin+ cells across all tumor sections (independent of treatment) and found a significant inverse correlation for both CD8 T- and NK cells (r2=−0.3, p=0.038 and r2=−0.33, p=0.026, respectively), but not CD4 T-cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A significant inverse correlation exists between NK cells and E-cadherin+ cells across all tumor sections.
source: To correlate immune infiltration against loss of tumor cells (a measure of local tumor control), we determined relationships between CD4 T-, CD8 T-, and NK cell populations and E-cadherin+ cells across all tumor sections (independent of treatment) and found a significant inverse correlation for both CD8 T- and NK cells (r2=−0.3, p=0.038 and r2=−0.33, p=0.026, respectively), but not CD4 T-cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No significant correlation exists between CD4 T-cells and E-cadherin+ cells across all tumor sections.
source: To correlate immune infiltration against loss of tumor cells (a measure of local tumor control), we determined relationships between CD4 T-, CD8 T-, and NK cell populations and E-cadherin+ cells across all tumor sections (independent of treatment) and found a significant inverse correlation for both CD8 T- and NK cells (r2=−0.3, p=0.038 and r2=−0.33, p=0.026, respectively), but not CD4 T-cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The proportion of infiltrating CD3-NK1.1+NKG2D+ cells (NKActive) was reduced under IR/CCR5iαPD1 combination treatment.
source: Surprisingly, the proportion of infiltrating CD3-NK1.1+NKG2D+ cells (NKActive) in stained tissue sections was reduced under IR/CCR5iαPD1 combination treatment, implying a decrease in total NK cell cytotoxic capacity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The reciprocal CD3-NK1.1+NKG2D- population increases upon triple combination treatment.
source: Indeed, the reciprocal CD3-NK1.1+NKG2D- population increases upon triple combination treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The hypoactive NKG2D- NK population (NKNKG2D-ve) is responsible for correlation of NK cells with E-cadherin loss with a superior inverse correlation (r2=0.52, p=0.003).
source: Surprisingly, the correlation of NK cells with decreased frequency of E-cadherin+ cells was completely abrogated with selection for more functionally competent NK cells (NKActive), implying that the opposite hypoactive NKG2D- NK population (NKNKG2D-ve) is responsible for correlation of NK cells with E-cadherin loss and indeed, a superior inverse correlation is observed for NKNKG2D-ve and E-cadherin compared to NKActive or NKTotal (r2=0.52, p=0.003) (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CD8 T-cells significantly segregated with E-cadherinlow, implying a contribution to tumor control.
source: While CD8 T-cells significantly segregated with E-cadherinlow, implying a contribution to tumor control, the association of NKNKG2D-ve was vastly more significant (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The association of NKNKG2D-ve with E-cadherinlow was vastly more significant than CD8 T-cells.
source: While CD8 T-cells significantly segregated with E-cadherinlow, implying a contribution to tumor control, the association of NKNKG2D-ve was vastly more significant (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: More than two-thirds of tumor-infiltrating NK cells expressed the canonical markers of tissue residency CD103 and CD49a.
source: Using a combination of uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) dimensionality reduction and manual gating, we found that more than two-thirds of tumor-infiltrating NK cells expressed the canonical markers of tissue residency CD103 and CD49a (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F), with the double positive population (hereafter referred to as bona fide trNK cells) being barely detectable in untreated mice and rising nearly 40-fold after treatment (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F, and Figure 4E.

claim: The double positive CD103+CD49a+ population (trNK cells) was barely detectable in untreated mice and rose nearly 40-fold after treatment.
source: Using a combination of uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) dimensionality reduction and manual gating, we found that more than two-thirds of tumor-infiltrating NK cells expressed the canonical markers of tissue residency CD103 and CD49a (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F), with the double positive population (hereafter referred to as bona fide trNK cells) being barely detectable in untreated mice and rising nearly 40-fold after treatment (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: trNK cells were less likely to be activated and expressed significantly lower levels of the activating receptors NKG2D and NKp46.
source: We then compared these two clusters and found that trNK were less likely to be activated and expressed significantly lower levels of the activating receptors NKG2D and NKp46, as well as significantly higher levels of the inhibitory receptor TIM-3 (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: trNK cells expressed significantly higher levels of the inhibitory receptor TIM-3.
source: We then compared these two clusters and found that trNK were less likely to be activated and expressed significantly lower levels of the activating receptors NKG2D and NKp46, as well as significantly higher levels of the inhibitory receptor TIM-3 (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: NK cells infiltrating tumors of mice treated with the IR/CCR5i/αPD1 combination were predominantly tissue resident and hypoactive, with a minority displaying a more conventional, fully active phenotype.
source: In line with our multiplex IF data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), these data indicate that NK cells infiltrating tumors of mice treated with the IR/CCR5i/αPD1 combination were predominantly tissue resident and hypoactive, with a minority displaying a more conventional, fully active phenotype.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: UMAP of the lymphocyte compartment did not delineate NK subpopulations and showed overlap with CD8 T-cells.
source: UMAP of the lymphocyte compartment did not delineate NK subpopulations and showed overlap with CD8 T-cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: UMAP of the CD8 and NK compartment alone led to three clear NK subpopulations: hypoactive (NK_C1), fully active (NK_C2), and cytotoxic (NK_C3) NK cells.
source: Therefore, we focused on UMAP of the CD8 and NK compartment alone, which led to three clear NK subpopulations that are distinct from CD8 T-cells and clearly separate out in clusters of hypoactive (NK_C1), fully active (NK_C2), and cytotoxic (NK_C3) NK cells from T-cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: NKG2D (KLRK1) expression was below detection across all CD8 and NK subpopulations retrieved from patient tumors.
source: In agreement with downregulation of circulating NKG2D+ in PDAC patients, NKG2D (KLRK1) expression was below detection across all CD8 and NK subpopulations retrieved from patient tumors (Groh et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of scRNA-seq data and supported by a citation to Groh et al., 2002.

claim: CD16high (FCGR3a) cytolytic NK cells (NK_C3) cluster separately from CD16- NK cells (NK_C1) which are more enriched for genes related to cytokine secretion than cytolytic function.
source: As expected, CD16high (FCGR3a) cytolytic NK cells (NK_C3) cluster separately from CD16- NK cells (NK_C1) which are more enriched for genes related to cytokine secretion than cytolytic function (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The NK_C1 cluster correlates best with the tissue-resident, hypoactive NK phenotype observed in mice as they displayed reduced cytolytic markers with additional expression of tissue residency markers CD103, CD49a, and the adaptive activating receptor NKG2C (KLRC2).
source: The NK_C1 cluster correlates best with the tissue-resident, hypoactive NK phenotype observed in mice as they similarly displayed reduced cytolytic (reduced NKG7, NKp80, GZMA, and PRF1) with additional expression of tissue residency markers CD103, CD49a, and the adaptive activating receptor NKG2C (KLRC2) (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The hypoactive NK_C1 cluster is enriched for CD56 but not CD16 expression.
source: Given that CD56 expression correlates with increased survival in PDAC patients (Figure 1C), we were intrigued to notice that the hypoactive NK_C1 cluster is enriched for CD56 but not CD16 expression (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The NK_C1 cluster represents a subset of NK cells in PDAC that display tissue residency markers (ITGAE, CD103 and ITGA1, CD49a) and have an immune-secretory phenotype (XCL1) as opposed to cytotoxic phenotype (NK_C2 CD16+, NKG7+).
source: These data suggest that the NK_C1 cluster represents a subset of NK cells in PDAC that display tissue residency markers (ITGAE, CD103 and ITGA1, CD49a) and have an immune-secretory phenotype (XCL1) as opposed to cytotoxic phenotype (NK_C2 CD16+, NKG7+) (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Verification of the NK_C1 population as trNK cells in a second scRNA-seq pancreatic cancer dataset of Peng et al., 2013, further supports the existence of these hypoactive cells in an independent PDAC cohort.
source: Verification of the NK_C1 population as trNK cells in a second scRNA-seq pancreatic cancer dataset of Peng et al., 2013, further supports the existence of these hypoactive cells in an independent PDAC cohort (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: The NK_C1 population had the highest expression of the chemokines XCL1 and XCL2.
source: The NK_C1 population had the highest expression of the chemokines XCL1 and XCL2, which have been demonstrated to attract cDC1 (Böttcher et al., 2018) and thereby increase cross-presentation to CD8+ T-cells.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of scRNA-seq data and supported by a citation to Böttcher et al., 2018.

claim: XCL1 and XCL2 have been demonstrated to attract cDC1 and thereby increase cross-presentation to CD8+ T-cells.
source: The NK_C1 population had the highest expression of the chemokines XCL1 and XCL2, which have been demonstrated to attract cDC1 (Böttcher et al., 2018) and thereby increase cross-presentation to CD8+ T-cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Böttcher et al., 2018.

claim: cDC1 cells are XCR1+ enriched compared to other DC subsets.
source: We next explored myeloid populations in the Steele et al. scPDAC dataset (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and identified cDC1 cells as XCR1+ enriched compared to other DC subsets (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: One of the main directions of communication from NK_C1 cells in PDAC is to cDC1 via XCR1.
source: As XCR1 is the receptor for XCL1/2, this suggests that one of the main directions of communication from NK_C1 cells in PDAC is to cDC1 (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: NK_C1-derived XCL1/2 is the strongest signal to XCR1+ cDC1s.
source: We again observed that NK_C1-derived XCL1/2 is the strongest signal to XCR1+ cDC1s (Figure 6C), supporting active crosstalk between NK_C1 and cDC1.
evidence: The claim is based on CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Analysis of specific ligand-receptor pairs between NK_C1 and 24 other cell groups yielded 32 significant interactions.
source: Analysis of specific ligand-receptor pairs between NK_C1 and 24 other cell groups yielded 32 significant interactions, of which the TNFSF14 (LIGHT)-TNFRSF14 pair was the most universal intercellular interaction, whereas CD74 (or MIF) signaling showed the highest communication probability (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Among the outgoing signals from different cell types, NK_C1 cells contributed the highest IL-16, CSF, LIGHT (TNFSF14), FASLG, and MIF signals in tumors.
source: Among the outgoing signals from different cell types, NK_C1 cells contributed the highest IL-16, CSF, LIGHT (TNFSF14), FASLG, and MIF signals in tumors (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is based on CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: IL-16 is mainly known as a chemoattractant for CD4+ T-cells, however CD4+ dendritic cells have also been demonstrated to be recruited by IL-16.
source: IL-16 is mainly known as a chemoattractant for CD4+ T-cells, however CD4+ dendritic cells have also been demonstrated to be recruited by IL-16 (Bialecki et al., 2011; Kaser et al., 1999; Vremec et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bialecki et al., 2011; Kaser et al., 1999; Vremec et al., 2000.

claim: IL-16 has the potential to induce MHC antigen presentation in CD4+ cells.
source: IL-16 has also been described to increase HLA-DR levels in CD4+ T-cells and eosinophils, indicating that it has the potential to induce MHC antigen presentation in CD4+ cells (Cruikshank et al., 1987; Rand et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cruikshank et al., 1987; Rand et al., 1991.

claim: trNK cells may improve tumor control via recruitment of cDC1 via XCR1, while promoting DC maturation via LIGHT-CD86 signaling and supporting DC antigen presentation to both CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells via MIF-CD74 signaling.
source: Taken together, these interactions support the hypothesis that trNK cells may improve tumor control via recruitment of cDC1 via XCR1, while promoting DC maturation via LIGHT-CD86 signaling (Zou and Hu, 2005) and supporting DC antigen presentation to both CD4+ and CD8+ T-cells via MIF-CD74 signaling (Basha et al., 2012; Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from CellChat analysis and supported by citations to Zou and Hu, 2005 and Basha et al., 2012.

claim: Dendritic cell-secreted BAG6 could promote both survival and cytokine release of NK cells by binding to NKp30.
source: On the other hand, dendritic cell-secreted BAG6 could promote both survival and cytokine release of NK cells by binding to NKp30 (Simhadri et al., 2008) and directly signal to CD8 T-cells via CXCL16-CXCR6 (Di Pilato et al., 2021; Vella et al., 2021), thereby generating an anti-tumor feedforward loop (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Simhadri et al., 2008; Di Pilato et al., 2021; Vella et al., 2021.

claim: IL-16 communicates to CD4+ Tregs, which could contribute to immunosuppression via enhanced Treg migration and expansion.
source: IL-16 also communicates to CD4+ Tregs, which could contribute to immunosuppression via enhanced Treg migration and expansion (Figure 6D; McFadden et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McFadden et al., 2007.

claim: Tregs may be susceptible to Fas-mediated cell death due to NK_C1 expression of Fas ligand.
source: However, Tregs may also be susceptible to Fas-mediated cell death due to NK_C1 expression of Fas ligand (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from CellChat analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A highly significant positive association exists between trNK and CD8 T infiltration in the murine orthotopic tumor model (R²=0.6571, p=0.003).
source: These results so far suggest the presence of immunoregulatory trNK cells in PDAC that are involved in an intricate immune communication network with DCs and CD8 T-cells to enhance anti-tumor immunity. To support this hypothesis, we explored the correlation between trNK and CD8 T infiltration in our murine orthotopic tumor model and found a highly significant positive association (R²=0.6571, p=0.003), which was strengthened when we focused on untreated (Mock) vs IR+IT combinations where trNK cells are evident (R²=0.9223, p=0.0004) (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The correlation between trNK and CD8 T infiltration was strengthened when focused on untreated (Mock) vs IR+IT combinations where trNK cells are evident (R²=0.9223, p=0.0004).
source: These results so far suggest the presence of immunoregulatory trNK cells in PDAC that are involved in an intricate immune communication network with DCs and CD8 T-cells to enhance anti-tumor immunity. To support this hypothesis, we explored the correlation between trNK and CD8 T infiltration in our murine orthotopic tumor model and found a highly significant positive association (R²=0.6571, p=0.003), which was strengthened when we focused on untreated (Mock) vs IR+IT combinations where trNK cells are evident (R²=0.9223, p=0.0004) (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: PDAC patient tumors with the lowest evidence for cDC1 involvement had a weak correlation of trNK_C1 with CD8A and CD8B (p=0.047; p=0.045, respectively).
source: PDAC patient tumors with the lowest evidence for cDC1 involvement had a weak correlation of trNK_C1 with CD8A and CD8B (p=0.047; p=0.045, respectively) which rises to a strong highly significant correlation when the highest levels of cDC1s are present (R=0.55, trNK_C1 vs CD8A p=0.0001; R=0.58, trNK_C1 vs CD8B p=0.000047) (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: PDAC patient tumors with the highest levels of cDC1s present had a strong highly significant correlation between trNK_C1 and CD8A (R=0.55, p=0.0001) and CD8B (R=0.58, p=0.000047).
source: PDAC patient tumors with the lowest evidence for cDC1 involvement had a weak correlation of trNK_C1 with CD8A and CD8B (p=0.047; p=0.045, respectively) which rises to a strong highly significant correlation when the highest levels of cDC1s are present (R=0.55, trNK_C1 vs CD8A p=0.0001; R=0.58, trNK_C1 vs CD8B p=0.000047) (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The benefit in overall survival of PDAC patients with radiotherapy is only apparent in the CD56low patient group (log-rank p<0.0001).
source: Indeed, separating PAAD_TCGA patients into those who received radiotherapy (RTx) vs those that did not showed that the benefit in overall survival of PDAC patients is only apparent in the CD56low patient group (log-rank p<0.0001, Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is based on survival analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Patients with tumors enriched for the trNK cell (NK_C1) gene signature were associated with improved PDAC survival compared to patients without trNK involvement.
source: Analysis of primary PDAC tumors from the TCGA (TCGA_PAAD) demonstrates that patients with tumors enriched for the trNK cell (NK_C1) gene signature were associated with improved PDAC survival compared to patients without trNK involvement (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on survival analysis shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Patients with trNKlow benefit from RTx (log-rank p<0.005).
source: Similarly to CD56low patients, we find that patients with trNKlow benefit from RTx (log-rank p<0.005, Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is based on survival analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: CCL5high patients (TCGA and CPTAC3) are significantly enriched for the trNK_C1 gene signature.
source: Notably, we find that despite an overall poor prognosis, CCL5high patients (TCGA and CPTAC3) are significantly enriched for the trNK_C1 gene signature (Figure 7), potentially due to strong CCR5 or CCR1-mediated recruitment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: CCL5high patients enriched for the NK_C1 signature or CD56 had significantly improved overall and disease-free survival.
source: Indeed, CCL5high patients enriched for the NK_C1 signature or CD56 had significantly improved overall and disease-free survival (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is based on survival analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Despite high CCL5 levels and an overall poor prognostic outcome, the presence of trNK cells significantly improves survival.
source: These results suggest that despite high CCL5 levels and an overall poor prognostic outcome, the presence of trNK cells significantly improves survival and provides an opportunity for intervention with the IR+IT combination.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from survival analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The majority of cancers with enriched expression of the NK_C1 gene signature showed improved survival (apart from endometrium and prostate).
source: The majority of cancers with enriched expression of our NK_C1 gene signature showed improved survival (Figure 8) (apart from endometrium and prostate) as a continuous variable or as a high vs low in a univariate Cox regression (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on pan-cancer survival analysis shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Enrichment of trNK cells is a protective factor across most solid malignancies.
source: The latter result supports our hypothesis that enrichment of trNK cells is a protective factor across most solid malignancies.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from pan-cancer survival analysis shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: trNK cells generally improve overall survival through improving CD8 T-cell activity in solid cancers.
source: Moreover, the ability to enrich for this population with IR+IT combinatorial strategies supports the idea that trNK cells generally improve overall survival though improving CD8 T-cell activity in solid cancers.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental and survival data presented.

claim: Novel strategies in preclinical PDAC models comprising IR, αPD1, and BMS-687681 (a dual CCR2/CCR5i) have shown promising increases in CD8 T-cells.
source: Novel strategies in preclinical PDAC models comprising IR, αPD1, and BMS-687681 (a dual CCR2/CCR5i) have shown promising increases in CD8 T-cells (Wang et al., 2022), whereas the combination of IR and the bifunctional agent αPD-1/IL-2Rβγ stimulates tumor penetration of polyfunctional stem-like activated CD8 T-cells and DNAM1+ cytotoxic NK cells (Piper et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2022.

claim: The combination of IR and the bifunctional agent αPD-1/IL-2Rβγ stimulates tumor penetration of polyfunctional stem-like activated CD8 T-cells and DNAM1+ cytotoxic NK cells.
source: Novel strategies in preclinical PDAC models comprising IR, αPD1, and BMS-687681 (a dual CCR2/CCR5i) have shown promising increases in CD8 T-cells (Wang et al., 2022), whereas the combination of IR and the bifunctional agent αPD-1/IL-2Rβγ stimulates tumor penetration of polyfunctional stem-like activated CD8 T-cells and DNAM1+ cytotoxic NK cells (Piper et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Piper et al., 2023.

claim: The use of IR alongside αPD-1/IL-2Rβγ or FAKi appeared to induce durable immunity in preclinical models.
source: In support of this, the use of IR alongside αPD-1/IL-2Rβγ or FAKi appeared to induce durable immunity in preclinical models (Lander et al., 2022; Piper et al., 2023), suggesting the induction of immunologic memory against tumor antigens is possible.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lander et al., 2022 and Piper et al., 2023.

claim: NK infiltration has been associated with positive outcomes in many solid tumors, considered to be due to the positive impact of cytotoxic NK cells in cytotoxic CD8 T-mediated tumor clearance.
source: NK infiltration has been associated with positive outcomes in many solid tumors, considered to be due to the positive impact of cytotoxic NK cells in cytotoxic CD8 T-mediated tumor clearance (Nersesian et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nersesian et al., 2021.

claim: In melanoma, NK-mediated expression of XCL1 is crucial for the migration of XCR1+ cDC1 and therefore the non-cytotoxic NK subsets in tumors may be vital for cDC1-mediated cross-presentation of tumor antigens to CD8 T-cells.
source: In melanoma, NK-mediated expression of XCL1 is crucial for the migration of XCR1+ cDC1 and therefore the non-cytotoxic NK subsets in tumors may be vital for cDC1-mediated cross-presentation of tumor antigens to CD8 T-cells (Böttcher et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Böttcher et al., 2018.

claim: NK-derived FLT3L correlated with increased cDC1 infiltration and improved overall survival and enhanced αPD1 treatment responses in melanoma.
source: NK-derived FLT3L correlated with increased cDC1 infiltration and improved overall survival and enhanced αPD1 treatment responses in melanoma (Barry et al., 2018), while intra-tumoral NK cells correlate with increased T-cell and dendritic cell infiltration and improved survival in neuroblastoma (Melaiu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barry et al., 2018.

claim: Intra-tumoral NK cells correlate with increased T-cell and dendritic cell infiltration and improved survival in neuroblastoma.
source: NK-derived FLT3L correlated with increased cDC1 infiltration and improved overall survival and enhanced αPD1 treatment responses in melanoma (Barry et al., 2018), while intra-tumoral NK cells correlate with increased T-cell and dendritic cell infiltration and improved survival in neuroblastoma (Melaiu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Melaiu et al., 2020.

claim: Combination therapy to stimulate an acute inflammatory response (IR) together with CCR5i/αPD1 (IT) sufficiently modulates the tumor immune microenvironment to improve tumor control.
source: Our data suggest that combination therapy to stimulate an acute inflammatory response (IR) together with CCR5i/αPD1 (IT) sufficiently modulates the tumor immune microenvironment to improve tumor control.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reduction of cancer cells correlates with intra-tumoral infiltration of NK cells (CD56brightCD16-) and improved CD8 T-cell penetration.
source: As frequently observed in solid tumors, reduction of cancer cells correlates with intra-tumoral infiltration of NK cells (CD56brightCD16-) and improved CD8 T-cell penetration (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2020.

claim: Adaptive NK cells were first identified as a subpopulation of blood-derived CD16+ NK cells in response to viral infection but more recently found to be independent of CD16 expression in lung tissue.
source: Adaptive NK cells were first identified as a subpopulation of blood-derived CD16+ NK cells in response to viral infection but more recently found to be independent of CD16 expression in lung tissue (Brownlie et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brownlie et al., 2021.

claim: Adaptive-like (i.e. NKG2C+) CD56brightCD16dim trNK cells have been identified in other epithelial sites such as the lungs.
source: While adaptive NK cells in the peripheral circulation are associated with a CD56dimCD16+ phenotype, adaptive-like (i.e. NKG2C+) CD56brightCD16dim trNK cells have been identified in other epithelial sites such as the lungs (Brownlie et al., 2021), therefore, our pancreatic tissue NK_C1 cells could comprise, at least in part, adaptive-like trNK cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brownlie et al., 2021.

claim: The inactivation of cytotoxic NK cells in tumors appears to be a conversion to immunomodulatory trNKs and perhaps an important mechanistic switch from innate to adaptive immunity.
source: Strikingly, using our trNK signature we find that elevated involvement of trNKs in PDAC correlates with CD8 T-cell recruitment in a cDC1-dependent manner (Figure 6G). Moreover, this supports a model where the inactivation of cytotoxic NK cells in tumors appears to be a conversion to immunomodulatory trNKs and perhaps an important mechanistic switch from innate to adaptive immunity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented.

claim: The therapeutic combination strategy of short ablative radiation-induced damage (IR) followed by CCR5i/αPD1 (IT) offers a potential regimen to increase disease-free survival in PDAC.
source: Our therapeutic combination strategy of short ablative radiation-induced damage (IR) followed by CCR5i/αPD1 (IT) offers a potential regimen to increase disease-free survival in PDAC.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: trNK-like cells with similar traits are increasingly being observed across a variety of cancers.
source: Likewise, trNK-like cells with similar traits are increasingly being observed across a variety of cancers (Brownlie et al., 2023; Kirchhammer et al., 2022; Marquardt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brownlie et al., 2023; Kirchhammer et al., 2022; Marquardt et al., 2015.

claim: The trNK signature identifies patients with a significant survival benefit across 14 tumor types.
source: Finally, our trNK signature identifies patients with a significant survival benefit across 14 tumor types, indicating a universal phenomenon attributable to this hypoactive, tissue-resident, immunomodulatory NK subset.
evidence: The claim is based on pan-cancer survival analysis shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.
